patient_note_history:
History 
HPI: A 61-year-old male complains of fatigue and weakness that started 6 months ago. He feels tired all day. He has a poor appetite and unintentionally lost 8 lbs in the past 6 months. He also complains of occasional nausea and vague, deep epigastric discomfort that radiates to the back. This discomfort started 4 months ago and has gradually increased to a severity of 4 out of 10. The discomfort decreases when he leans forward and increases when he lies on his back. There is no relationship of the discomfort to food. No changes in bowel movement regularity, but he has recently noticed more foul-smelling, greasy-looking stools. He denies blood in the stool. He feels sad sometimes, has lost interest in things that he used to enjoy, wakes up unusually early in the morning, and complains of low energy and poor concentration that have affected his daily activities and work. The patient denies suicidal ideation or plans. No feelings of guilt or worthlessness. 
ROS: Negative except as above. 
Allergies: NKDA. 
Medications: Tylenol. 
PMH: None. 
PSH: Appendectomy at 16 years old. 
SH: He smoked 1 pack per day for 30 years; stopped 6 months ago. Drinks 2 beers daily and 3-4 beers on weekends. He is sexually active with his wife. 
FH: Father died accidentally with diabetes. Mother died from breast cancer.

exam_lines.source_text: Patient is in no acute distress, looks sad.
HEENT: No conjunctival pallor, mouth and pharynx are normal.
Neck: Supple, no JVD, no lymphadenopathy, thyroid within normal limits (WNL).

Abdomen: Soft, nondistended, mild epigastric tenderness, no rebound tenderness, positive Murphy's sign, bowel sounds x 4, no hepatosplenomegaly.

gold_additional_diagnosis:
• Peptic ulcer disease: Suspect this diagnosis in any patient with epigastric pain, although the complaint is neither sensitive nor specific enough to make a reliable diagnosis. It is important to note that many patients deny any relationship of the pain to meals. Weight loss, however, is unusual in uncomplicated ulcer disease and may suggest gastric malignancy. 

• Hypothyroidism: Nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue and weakness may suggest this common diagnosis. Abdominal pain is unusual.

Opening Scenario:

William Jordan, a 61-year-old male, comes to the office complaining of fatigue.

Vital Signs:

- BP: 135/85 mm Hg
- Temp: 98.6°F (37°C)
- RR: 13/minute
- HR: 70/minute, regular

Examinee Tasks:

1. Take a focused history.
2. Perform a focused physical exam (do not perform rectal, genitourinary, or female breast exam).
3. Explain your clinical impression and workup plan to the patient.
4. Write the patient note after leaving the room.

Checklist/SP Sheet:

Patient Description:

- Patient: a 61-year-old male, married with three children.

Notes for the SP:

- Look weak and sad and lean forward while seated.
- Exhibit abdominal discomfort that increases when you lie on your back.
- Show pain on palpation of the epigastric area.

Challenging Questions to Ask:

"I will be on vacation with my wife. Can we arrange to conduct the tests upon my return?"

Examinee Response:

"It doesn't sound as though you're feeling well enough to be able to enjoy a trip. We'll conduct some preliminary blood tests, after which we'll assess your condition to determine if it's appropriate for you to be discharged.."

Examinee Checklist:

Entrance:

- Examinee knocked on the door before entering.
- Examinee made eye contact with the SP.
- Examinee correctly spelled the patient's name.
- Examinee introduced themself by name.
- Examinee identified their role or position.

Reflective Listening:

- The examinee asked an open-ended question and actively listened to the response.
- The examinee asked the SP to list their concerns and listened to the response without interrupting.
- The examinee summarized the SP's concerns, often using the SP's own words.

Information Gathering:

- Examinee elicited data efficiently and accurately.

Connecting With the Patient:

- Examinee recognized the SP's emotions and responded with PEARLS.

Sample Closure:

"Mr. Jordan, your symptoms are consistent with a few conditions. They may be caused by an ulcer that would resolve with a course of antibiotics and acid suppressors, or they may have a more serious cause, such as pancreatic cancer. I am going to schedule you for an abdominal CT scan that may reveal the source of your pain, and I will also run some blood tests. I understand your worries regarding your upcoming vacation; however, the results of your tests should arrive in a few days and will provide us with a clear assessment of your current condition.. In the interim, our social worker is available to assist you in identifying strategies to manage the stress you have been facing in your life.. "Are there any inquiries you'd like to make?"
